This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. text:
This chapter addresses branch management and pruning of young jackfruit trees before they come into significant fruiting, aimed at building a strong, well-shaped, productive tree structure. The text explains that unmanaged jackfruit trees tend to grow tall with fruit setting high in the canopy, which is both harder to harvest and puts more mechanical strain on branches; deliberate early pruning/training is recommended to encourage a lower, more open, well-branched framework so that more fruit forms within easier reach and on stronger, better-supported wood.

Practical guidance given includes removing weak, crossing, or diseased branches early, selecting and encouraging a small number of well-spaced main scaffold branches rather than allowing dense, congested growth, and controlling overall tree height by heading back the leading shoot(s) once the tree has established the desired framework. The chapter also discusses the connection between pruning and light penetration: an overly dense canopy shades inner branches, reducing their ability to flower and fruit well, so opening up the canopy is presented as directly beneficial to fruit yield and quality, not just to tree shape.

The chapter notes that pruning cuts should be made cleanly and, where appropriate, treated or protected to reduce the risk of disease or pest entry at the wound, and that major structural pruning is best carried out while the tree is still young, since large cuts on an older, already-fruiting tree are more disruptive and slower to heal.
